$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing under src/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for WIN-258 TRANCHE 3 — tenancy's five driven ports that
are not the repository. One entry per lock, per transaction-scope check, per
compare-and-set precondition, per projection and per cryptographic property,
each carrying the file it lives in, the EXACT text that implements it
(`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), and the NAMED cases that were seen
IT IS A THIRD FILE BESIDE mutations.json AND mutations-identity.json rather
than an extension of either, because the three tranches are three separate
claims about three separate port surfaces and a reader checking one should
not have to read past the other two. The three are hashed by the same
packages.adapters.config rule and counted together by the v1 ledger.
WHY THIS TRANCHE NEEDED ITS OWN SWEEP MORE THAN THE OTHER TWO. Four of these
five ports return a boolean, a small number, or nothing at all. Every one of
them is trivially correct in memory and the interesting half — whether the
lock BLOCKS, whether the counter's read-modify-write is atomic, whether the
digest is a shape PostgreSQL will accept — is invisible to any assertion on a
returned value. A guard nothing can turn red is a guard that is not there,
and in this tranche most of the guards are of exactly that kind.
procedure: PROVE THE SUITES GREEN FIRST. Tranche 1's first sweep reported 22 kills and
every one was VACUOUS: a context's `dist` had been cleaned, so every suite
failed to load its import and would have 'died' against any mutation at all,
including none. The driver runs each suite set UNMUTATED and refuses to sweep
unless it is green with a non-zero test count, and classifies a run with no
executed cases as VACUOUS rather than as a kill.
For one entry: replace its `from` with its `to` in the named file (the driver
requires the `from` to occur EXACTLY ONCE, so a stale entry is an error and
not a silent no-op), run the named suites against a real PostgreSQL container,
and confirm a NAMED case in `kills` is among the failures. Then revert and
confirm green again.
EIGHTEEN OF THE TWENTY-ONE NEED A REAL POSTGRESQL, and none of those eighteen
could have been written against a double: M-P01, M-P05 and M-P08 are about
whether a statement BLOCKS, which is not a value; M-P02, M-P03 and M-P09 are
about a WHERE clause that has to be the thing doing the filtering; M-P04,
M-P07, M-P12 and M-P14 are about a client resolved through the caller's named
transaction rather than the pool; M-P10 is a null the schema cannot express;
M-P11 is a statement COUNT; M-P13, M-P15 and M-P16 are about rows only
identity-access's stores can produce; and M-P21 is what happens when two
halves of one adapter are given two ambient frames. The three that do NOT
need one are M-P18, M-P19 and M-P20, all on the token issuer, which is the
one port of the five with no database in it.
THREE FINDINGS CAME OUT OF WRITING THIS SWEEP AND ARE RECORDED IN THE
ENTRIES THEMSELVES rather than only in prose: `pg_advisory_xact_lock` returns
`void` and the client cannot deserialize a `void` column (the first
integration run refused); the constant a lock statement naturally projects,
`SELECT 1`, is the pattern the sibling statement-count suites use to discard
the driver's connection probe, so the advisory lock was measured at ZERO
statements until the projection changed; and the in-memory
`InvitationTokenIssuer` the context ships mints a digest
`OrganizationInvitation_tokenHash_check` refuses, which every use-case suite
in the tree passes with.

result: TWENTY-ONE ENTRIES, TWENTY-ONE KILLS, NONE VACUOUS, on a real PostgreSQL
container at branch head. Each kill is a NAMED case in the `kills` list of
its entry. The driver proved all SEVEN distinct suite sets green before it
mutated anything -- 12, 19, 10, 7, 18, 14 and 7 executed cases -- and
classified nothing as vacuous, because a run that executes no cases is
reported as VACUOUS rather than as a kill.
NOTHING SURVIVED, AND THAT IS WORTH ONE SENTENCE OF SUSPICION rather than
a victory lap: it is what a sweep looks like when the suites were written
AFTER the guards and aimed at them. The two entries that would have
survived a weaker suite are the ones to look at. M-P01, M-P05 and M-P08
remove the BLOCKING from the three locks and change no returned value at
all, so only an assertion on the ORDER of events across two concurrent
transactions can see them; and M-P11 turns one atomic increment into a
read-modify-write that returns exactly the same number, so only a statement
COUNT can see it. Both kinds of case exist here because the first drafts of
this tranche had neither.
THREE FINDINGS FELL OUT OF THE WORK RATHER THAN OUT OF THE SWEEP, and each
is recorded at the line it concerns:
`pg_advisory_xact_lock` returns `void` and the client cannot deserialize a
`void` column. The first integration run refused with 'Failed to
deserialize column of type void'. The call is now a one-row function scan
in FROM, and `pg_locks` was checked directly to confirm the lock is still
taken.
The constant that scan then projected, `SELECT 1`, is the pattern the
sibling statement-count suites use to discard the driver's connection
probe -- so the one lock of the three whose return value proves nothing was
also measured at ZERO statements. Caught by the N+1 pin. The projection is
now `true` and this tranche's filter anchors the probe pattern.
The in-memory `InvitationTokenIssuer` the context ships mints
`digest:plt_inv_1`, which `OrganizationInvitation_tokenHash_check` refuses.
Every use-case suite in the tree passes with it. Pinned on BOTH stores in
`ports-conformance.integration.test.ts`, with PostgreSQL's own refusal
beside it.
